## P9-4.6 rigorous audit

**Disposition: HOLD for one runtime correctness correction and two evidence/boundary corrections.**

P9-4.6 is otherwise strong. I found no reason to reopen accepted P9-4.5, and the snapshot/restoration architecture itself is substantially sound. The main defect is narrower: **reset/rebase can publish before their lifecycle-receipt semantics have been independently cross-validated.**

| Surface                                            | Verdict                     | Reason                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| P9-4.5 entry/baseline                              | **PASS**                    | Accepted baseline and uploaded 4.6 source bindings agree.                                                                   |
| Snapshot content/identity                          | **PASS**                    | Closed implementation envelope, constituent frozen schemas, complete reference/profile/state/reset/ledger/commit preimages. |
| Restoration/readmission                            | **PASS**                    | Reconstructs rather than trusts identities; fresh C/reset/reference admission precedes exposure.                            |
| `set_state()` boundary                             | **PASS**                    | Current C only; clock, graph/profile/context, reset, Q and ledger cannot be replaced.                                       |
| Reset/rebase scientific effect                     | **PASS**                    | Correct current-vs-baseline distinction and live-clock preservation.                                                        |
| Deep independence/concurrency                      | **PASS**                    | Detached snapshots, independently reconstructed duplicates, immutable retained state, atomic pointer observations.          |
| Historical structural checks                       | **PASS within 4.6 ceiling** | Strong coherent-rehash, ordering, clock and receipt-shape pressure without pretending to authenticate historical truth.     |
| **Reset/rebase prepublication receipt validation** | **FAIL / BLOCKER**          | Semantic receipt checks exist on later restoration, but not before the live administrative state is published.              |
| Clock-correction evidence                          | **HOLD**                    | Important positive post-fix cases are supplementary rather than in the retained 76-test source-bound run.                   |
| `P9-7.1-C_OS` accounting                           | **NARROW**                  | Must distinguish bounded 4.6 replay evidence from the stronger 4.7a receipt/replay cycle.                                   |

### What passed particularly well

The serialization architecture is appropriately conservative. `cos_snapshot_payload()` does **not** pretend that the release supplied a top-level frozen snapshot schema: it introduces an implementation-specific closed layout while continuing to validate the actual scientific/reset/lifecycle/commit constituent schemas. It also defensively copies I-JSON input and requires exact family/version/layout markers. 

`from_state()` is much stronger than a hash checker. It reconstructs the reference geometry and complete profile from content, checks scientific/reset/lifecycle identities, restores and checks commit preimages against the ordered ledger, rebuilds `GeometryStageInputs`, demands byte-equivalence to the reconstructed scientific/reset preimages, and finally performs fresh C_OS zero-duration current/reset/reference admission before creating the receiver. No restored object is exposed before that chain succeeds.  This is aligned with the V4 requirement that restoration reconstruct and **re-admit** the lifecycle identity rather than merely deserialize it. 

The hostile-snapshot pressure is also good. The tests don't stop at stale hashes: they coherently rehash changes to graph/profile/context/Q/state, exercise native singular current/reset states, attack every nested reference identity, reorder/drop/duplicate historical commits and receipts, and alter historical clocks after coherently recomputing commit IDs.  The discovery during development—an earlier commit at `0.5` followed by one at `0.25`—was a useful genuine pressure result, and the importer now has an explicit local clock-transition rule. 

`set_state()` is also properly narrow. It cannot smuggle in a new clock, graph, orientation, profile, context, reset, charge target or receipt history; it reconstructs the proposed C state and reruns state admission before a single `_OwnedCOS` publication. That matches the normative distinction between current-state assignment and full restoration.  

Deep independence is convincing: snapshot mutation, duplicate/copy/deepcopy mutation, retained old-state immutability, nested receipt mutation, reference-map mutation, and a concurrent snapshot during an administrative operation are all pressured. 

I also independently checked the submitted evidence binding. The three uploaded changed files hash exactly to the execution record's override hashes:

* lifecycle: `52a3e365...432c89e`
* codec: `90ee2f9c...89dde3`
* test owner: `2f2da3ef...ddcdc`

The uploaded test source contains exactly **23 `CandidateCOSLifecycleTests` methods and 23 inherited `CandidateCOSOperationTests` methods**, matching the record, and the three Python files compile. The 4.6 baseline also exactly matches the accepted 4.5 baseline `ec9f8662...`.  

---

## Blocker: administrative receipt semantics are checked too late

This is the important finding.

`reset()` and `rebase_reset_baseline()` correctly do all their scientific work provisionally:

$$
\text{old state}
\rightarrow
\text{proposed reset/rebase state}
\rightarrow
\text{readmission}
\rightarrow
\text{receipt payloads}
\rightarrow
\text{commit}
\rightarrow
\text{target lifecycle state}.
$$

But after `make_commit_receipts()` and `_lifecycle_state()`, `_administrative()` goes directly to:

```text
publication = _OwnedCOS(...)
self._owned = publication
```

There is **no analogue of the ordinary-operation `bind_step_result()`** and no invocation of the semantic rules later implemented by `_restore_commits()` before that pointer swap. 

That matters because `make_commit_receipts()` establishes schema/content identity, not the lifecycle truth of fields such as:

* reset `reset_baseline_digest == source_reset_digest == target_reset_digest`;
* rebase `old_reset_digest/new_reset_digest` exactly matching the actual reset transition;
* rebase preserving current authority;
* local parent convention;
* correct receipt slot meanings;
* historical reset-chain continuity;
* candidate/carrier disposition semantics.

Those stronger relationships are indeed checked—but only when a snapshot is subsequently loaded by `_restore_commits()`. 

So there is presently an undesirable state:

$$
\boxed{
\text{live administrative commit acceptance}
<
\text{later snapshot restoration acceptance}
}
$$

A schema-valid internal construction error could therefore produce a **successfully published live state whose own snapshot cannot subsequently be restored**.

For example, imagine an internal regression that constructs a reset receipt with a syntactically valid but wrong `reset_baseline_digest`. The receipt can still receive a valid receipt ID and commit ID because its hashes faithfully identify those wrong bytes. `_lifecycle_state()` does not care about that reset-receipt-specific relation. The pointer is published. Later `_restore_commits()` rejects exactly that contradiction.

The V4 lifecycle contract requires receipt/lifecycle postconditions to be part of the atomic admission boundary, not something discovered only at later reload. 

### Required correction

I would introduce one shared semantic checker for a **local committed delta**, used both:

$$
\text{live reset/rebase}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\text{snapshot restoration}.
$$

Something conceptually like:

$$
V_{\rm lifecycle}
(
X_{\rm source},
X_{\rm target},
\text{commit},
\Delta R,
\text{operation kind}
)
$$

should validate the relationships currently scattered through `_restore_commits()` before `_owned` changes.

Then pressure it with **schema-valid semantic corruption**, not just exceptions. The existing `test_all_administrative_faults_keep_state_and_commit_preimages_atomic` is strong for thrown failures, but it patches helpers to *raise*.  Add controls where receipt/commit construction succeeds while returning, for example, a wrong-but-well-formed reset digest, swapped rebase digests, wrong authoritative equality, wrong parent, or wrong history subject. The operation must reject/raise **before publication**.

This is the only runtime defect I would make acceptance-blocking.

---

## Evidence correction: put the clock fix into the retained run

The clock bug found during development was substantive enough that I would not leave its positive boundary controls as supplementary prose evidence.

The retained source-bound capture has 76 tests and includes the coherent-rehash **negative** clock-transition test. But the execution record separately lists three positive checks involving zero then minimum-subnormal positive duration at starting times `0`, `0.125`, and `1e308`; those checks are explicitly outside the retained focused run. 

Because this was a newly discovered correctness defect, move those cases into a proper `CandidateCOSLifecycleTests` method, add it to `_P946_METHODS`, and rerun the focused capture.

That would make the evidence topology:

$$
\text{bug found}
\rightarrow
\text{implementation correction}
\rightarrow
\boxed{\text{source-bound negative + positive regression}}
$$

rather than ending in an unretained supplementary check.

I consider this an **acceptance-evidence requirement**, not another runtime blocker.

---

## Boundary correction: `P9-7.1-C_OS`

The planning documents deliberately separate these leaves:

* **P9-4.6** — snapshot/load/reset/rebase/deep-copy;
* **P9-4.7a** — atomic failure, receipt ownership, and the stronger state→step→snapshot→restore→replay pressure. 

At the same time, the registered `P9-7.1-C_OS` alias of 4.6 was described as “Snapshot/load/replay, ordinary reset/rebase and duplication.” 

The present 4.6 suite actually does contain a useful **bounded replay witness**: after a step and rebase, a duplicate/restored receiver receives the same next request and reaches exactly the same target/commit.  So I do not think the alias itself is wrong.

But the execution record should make the distinction explicit:

$$
\boxed{
\text{P9-7.1-C\_OS bounded snapshot/continuation evidence}
}
$$

is supplied by 4.6, while

$$
\boxed{
\text{integrated receipt-ownership + failure + replay pressure}
}
$$

remains P9-4.7a.

The fixture catalog itself keeps `SNAPSHOT-LOAD-REPLAY` and `RECEIPT-OWNERSHIP` as distinct lifecycle cases, which supports exactly that separation. 

I would therefore change the bare `evidence_aliases: ["P9-7.1-C_OS"]` wording or add a disposition field saying the alias covers the bounded P9-7.1 portion only and creates **no 4.7a credit**.

---

## One conceptual instruction for P9-4.7a

Do not accidentally redefine “replay” to mean “reconstruct the complete trajectory from all commit records.”

P9-4.6 correctly permits `set_state()` to change current C without manufacturing a commit while preserving the existing ledger and clock.  Consequently:

$$
\text{last historical commit target state}
\neq
\text{live current state}
$$

is lawful after `set_state()`.

So 4.7a needs to distinguish:

$$
\text{snapshot continuation replay}
$$

—restore the exact current scientific/lifecycle identity, supply the same future input, obtain the same future result—

from

$$
\text{historical provenance replay from origin}.
$$

The latter is impossible in general while unreceipted `set_state()` remains lawful, because commit history intentionally does not encode that assignment. That is not a 4.6 defect; it is a claim boundary 4.7a should preserve.

---

### Evidence-package note

The execution record binds `P9-4.6-Review.md` by SHA-256, but that review file was not among the submitted 4.6 uploads and I could not locate it in the available File Library search.  That doesn't alter the code findings above, but I cannot independently approve that particular review-file binding from the submitted package.

### Bottom line

P9-4.6 is **close and scientifically well designed**. Snapshot reconstruction, reference-map authority, current/reset re-admission, `set_state`, deep immutability, canonical save/load, coherent-hash attacks, and bounded continuation replay all look right.

My acceptance conditions are:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
1.&\ \text{validate reset/rebase receipt semantics before publication;}\\
2.&\ \text{move the post-clock-fix positive regressions into the source-bound capture;}\\
3.&\ \text{narrow/clarify P9-7.1-C\_OS credit versus P9-4.7a.}
\end{aligned}
}
$$

After those, I would expect **P9-4.6 to pass without reopening any earlier Tranche-4 dynamics work**.
